column4: At the sacred-valley encounter, God identifies Himself and commands Moses to worship Him and establish prayer, linking mountain revelation to the worship commanded in the secure city.
Still at the fire encounter, Moses is told to take the staff and not fear, adding another direct fear-to-reassurance movement at Tūr.
After speaking to Moses at the mountain, God says He chose him through His messages and speech, explicitly naming the revelatory privilege of the encounter.
God writes exhortation and explanation for Moses on the tablets, giving the mountain revelation a concrete covenantal form.
Moses chooses seventy people for God's appointed meeting, where an earthquake seizes them and he pleads for mercy; Tūr is thereby a collective meeting marked by fear and dependence.
God promises to strengthen Moses through Aaron and give them authority so their enemies cannot reach them, extending the mountain encounter's assurance of safety into the mission.
God answers Moses' fear with a refusal of that feared outcome and promises to remain with the messengers listening, another assurance flowing from the divine call.
The winter and summer journeys place repeated travel outside the city immediately before the command to worship the Lord of the House and the gift of security.
The believers may not violate God's rites, sacred times, offerings, or those heading to the Sacred House, so approach to the House is protected by explicit boundaries.
The prohibition on polytheists approaching the Sacred Mosque gives a literal sacred boundary to the section's secondary image of approaching a dwelling's precinct.
Towns are not destroyed until a messenger recites God's signs in their mother settlement, making the city a center of revelation, civic responsibility, and judgment.
The people of the towns are asked whether they felt secure from punishment arriving by night while they slept, exposing the limit of civic safety before divine judgment.
The matching question asks whether the towns felt secure from punishment arriving by day while they played, completing the night-and-day challenge to assumed safety.
The passage asks whether they felt secure from God's plan and says only the losers do so, directly distinguishing true security from presumption.
Those on earth are asked whether they feel secure from the earth being made to swallow them, challenging safety that rests only on one's present place.
A second question asks whether they feel secure from a storm of stones, extending the warning that earthly enclosure cannot guarantee safety from judgment.
Whoever brings a good deed is promised better and security from the terror of that Day, joining good action, final recompense, and the security root.
The Trust is offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains, which shrink from it in fear, while the human bears it; mountain, human, fear, and a different ءمن sense meet in one ayah.
A man runs from the farthest edge of the city and urges his people to follow the messengers, making the bounded city's periphery part of a revelation scene.
Entry is allowed into houses that are not inhabited when they contain some use, explicitly distinguishing an occupied social dwelling from an uninhabited structure.
In the judgment announced after the oath by Tūr, the mountains themselves move away, reversing the fixed mountain-place invoked at the opening.
After the Prophet is driven out, the cave becomes a place of companionship, divine tranquility, and unseen support, reversing the expectation that safety lies only in his inhabited city.
The Prophet's own town is named as the town that expelled him, while stronger towns were destroyed, setting residence and civic strength against their inability to secure either people or place.
People are expelled unjustly from their homes, and divine defense preserves monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, linking lost dwelling-security with protection of sacred places.
The wrongdoers' houses stand empty because of their wrongdoing, giving the section's image of a place with no one in it a judgmental civic form.
After the wind's destruction, nothing of the people is visible except their dwellings, turning an inhabited place into houses without inhabitants.
Lot is told to leave with his household by night before the city's punishment, and the assurance “Is not morning near?” joins home-leaving, judgment, أليس, and nearness.
The question أَوَلَيْسَ asks whether the Creator of the heavens and earth can create their like, paralleling surah 95's closing appeal from human creation to divine judgment.
The question أَوَلَيْسَ asks whether the One who created the heavens and earth can revive the dead, another exact creation-to-resurrection counterpart to 95:8.
The punishment announced as the answer to the Mount's oath has no one able to avert it, adding the certainty pressed by the section's final judgment question.
Quraysh's settled familiarity introduces the journeys, House, food, and safety that follow, giving the inhabited community a social cohesion before its movement beyond the city.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations and ask acceptance, contributing the physical establishment of the sacred center invoked in 2:125-126.
Fighting at the Sacred Mosque is forbidden unless aggression begins there, showing both the sanctuary's protective boundary and the condition under which it can be breached.
The command to turn toward the Sacred Mosque, wherever the believers are, makes the House an orienting center for people located both within and beyond the city.
Prayer is maintained while in fear during movement and remembered fully once secure, pairing fear and safety with travel and settled worship.
The command to “perceive” sound judgment in orphans uses the same ءنس perception branch as Moses noticing the fire, confirming that the section's lexical bridge is not confined to sight of flame.
Men from humankind seek refuge with men from the jinn and receive greater burden, joining the human-jinn distinction to a failed search for safety.
After leaving the city, Moses turns toward Midian and asks his Lord to guide him on the right way, contributing the exposed journey between civic fear and later refuge.
Moses explains that he fears being killed for his earlier act, supplying the concrete danger answered by God's protection in 28:35.
At the divine commission Moses voices fear that the people will deny him, supplying the fear to which the assurance in 26:15 responds.
One who leaves home for God finds many refuges and abundance in the earth, giving a positive Quranic counterimage to blameworthy refusal to leave one's house.
Thousands leave their homes fearing death, yet God causes them to die and then revives them, tying house-leaving and fear to the limits of worldly safety and to resurrection.
The stones that destroy Lot's town are said not to be far from other wrongdoers, continuing 11:81's near-far language as a warning beyond one city.
At judgment the disbelievers ask to believe, but the ayah asks how faith can be reached from a far place, making distance an image of belated access.
They had disbelieved before and cast conjectures from a far place, explaining the moral distance named in 34:52.
The command to listen for the caller from a near place connects nearness and divine calling to the day of emergence.
The greatest terror does not grieve the rewarded, and angels welcome them to the promised Day, extending fear-to-security into the final meeting.
The Prophet's opponents nearly uproot him from the land, after which they themselves would remain only briefly, showing the insecurity of residence under civic rejection.
The Prophet asks for truthful entrance and exit and for supporting authority, joining movement between places to the section's city-and-rule secondary connection.
Immediately before the call from the Mount, Moses is identified as chosen, messenger, and prophet, specifying the addressee whom God brings near in 19:52.
The people questioned about being left secure are specifically surrounded by gardens and springs; this ayah supplies the cultivated setting rather than 26:146 itself.
Crops and palms with tender fruit continue the settled provision scene before the mountain houses of 26:149.
